Introduction Antitakeover provisions (ATPs) are a contentious topic in corporate governance research. Prior research held that ATPs tend to harm firm value because they partially insulate managers from takeover threats (Gompers et al. (2003), Bebchuk et al. (2009)). Two influential studies, Masulis et al. (2007) and Harford et al. (2012), argue that the firm value discount due to ATPs comes largely from acquisitions of the empire-building type by entrenched managers. More recently, however, a growing literature has concluded that ATPs may actually be beneficial for firms in various contexts. One of the first studies is Chemmanur et al. (2011). They find that, in the context of IPOs, firms with better management quality and more ATPs outperform their peer firms both in terms of IPO valuation and post-IPO performance. Relatedly, Johnson et al. (2015) argue that ATPs can lead to higher IPO valuations and post-IPO performance because they help to credibly bond firms' commitments to their business partners. Similarly, Cen et al. (2016) document that ATPs can help firms that have corporate customers as important stakeholders achieve superior performance by strengthening their customer relationship. ATPs also increase firm value in hard-to-value industries (Humphery-Jenner (2014)) and for firms with low bargaining power as potential takeover targets (Stráska and Waller (2010)). Finally, Chemmanur and Tian (2018) use a regression discontinuity analysis to show that firms with more ATPs not only generate more patents, but more high-quality patents, indicating a causal effect of ATPs on innovation. Our research contributes to this literature in two primary ways. First, our paper presents the first study of ATPs in Germany, a corporate governance system that has often been compared to that in the U.S. (Shleifer and Vishny (1997), Allen and Gale (2001), Hopt (2015)). Because most ATP studies are based on U.S. firms, we believe our study provides important complementary evidence. As forcefully shown by Karpoff and Wittry (2018), the institutional context is key to inferences in corporate governance studies. Second, our study is the first to show that firms make better acquisitions if they have more and stronger ATPs in their corporate charters. The evidence contrasts starkly with that presented in the two benchmark studies of U.S. firms by Masulis et al. (2007) and Harford et al. (2012). We draw on Chemmanur and Jiao's (2012) excellent theoretical framework to develop testable hypotheses for the ATP-value relation in the German context. Their theoretical model goes beyond that of Stein, 1988, Stein, 1989, who establishes the possibility of managerial short-termism driven by asymmetric information. Chemmanur and Jiao (2012) demonstrate that, in an environment with asymmetric information about management quality, dual-class share structures and other ATPs may be value-enhancing in the presence of talented managers. Accordingly, their long-term value creation hypothesis establishes relations among the quality of a firm's management, the prevalence of ATPs in its corporate charter, and long-run value creation. We thus rely on Chemmanur and Jiao's (2012) framework in our research context to derive several hypotheses about the value creation by acquiring firms with a higher number of ATPs, as well as its specific sources. Our overarching hypothesis is that, in the German institutional setting, firms with more and stronger ATPs create value in acquisitions. We derive this prediction in large part from the institutional feature that German firms historically relied less on external control mechanisms. Despite many recent corporate governance reforms that aimed to improve external control mechanisms, such as the European Takeover Directive, which sought to increase external control contestability (see Dissanaike et al. (2019)), internal control mechanisms such as a two-tier board structure, blockholder monitoring, and co-determination of the supervisory board remain dominant features in the typical German firm (Goergen et al. (2008)). These internal control mechanisms create effective management accountability vis-á-vis important stakeholders in the firm. Because of their power to withdraw their contributions to the firm, as argued by Acharya et al. (2011), these stakeholders can efficiently discipline managers. Therefore, while there is some evidence of the long-run value-creating effects of ATPs in the U.S. (Chemmanur et al. (2011), Johnson et al. (2015), Cen et al. (2016), Chemmanur and Tian (2018)), these effects may be even more pronounced in the German institutional setting, given the lower reliance on external control mechanisms.1 For our empirical analyses, we hand-collected data on thirty-six ATPs for a sample of public firms in Germany. This dataset allows us to reconstruct the widely used corporate governance indices such as the G-Index (Gompers et al. (2003)), the E-Index as well as the O-Index (Bebchuk et al. (2009)), and the C-Index Harford et al. (2012)). The empirical results confirm our main hypothesis that entrenchment indices are significant drivers of acquirers' cumulative abnormal announcement returns (CAARs). On average, ATPs have a positive valuation effect, i.e., acquirer announcement returns are higher in firms with stronger takeover defenses. As in Harford et al. (2012), we observe that the C-Index better explains CAARs than the E-Index. In all subsequent analyses, we thus focus on the C-Index, which is defined by the sum of dummy variables for a classified board structure (vis-à-vis a staggered board structure for the E-Index), a supermajority regarding transaction voting, limits on amending corporate charters and bylaws, golden parachutes, and poison pills. With the coming of the era of decentralized ownership in China’s capital market, ATP adoption has become more important and attracted more attention. Also, investors focus more on pricing efficiency. Antitakeover provisions relate to managerial entrenchment primarily by reducing takeover pressure and thereby increasing managerial control over the firm. The core mechanism is that provisions such as poison pills, golden parachutes, staggered boards, and classified boards make it harder for outside bidders to acquire control, which reduces the threat of replacement and strengthens managers’ ability to retain power [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R4][N1-R5]. Poison pills are especially direct because they are defensive tactics explicitly designed to deter hostile bids [N1-R1][N1-R4]. Golden parachutes also reduce takeover pressure by providing managers with generous compensation packages if they are terminated in a takeover, which can discourage bidders or make the acquisition less attractive [N1-R5]. Staggered and classified boards affect board election by making it harder for shareholders to replace directors, which can slow the takeover process and increase managerial strategic power [N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-R5].

The evidence on how each provision changes board election and strategic power is mixed in the literature. Classified boards are said to make it harder for shareholders to replace directors, thereby increasing managerial entrenchment, but the cited evidence also suggests that classified boards do not clearly entrench managers in takeover bidding or facilitate self-dealing in that context [N2-R1]. Staggered boards similarly delay the replacement of directors, which can reinforce managerial control, but the evidence here is not presented as definitive proof of entrenchment in all cases [N2-R1]. Poison pills and golden parachutes are more directly linked to managerial entrenchment because they alter the cost and attractiveness of acquisitions, while staggered and classified boards are more about changing the mechanics of board elections [N2-R1][N1-R2][N1-R5].

Entrenchment is measured in the literature through several approaches. One common method is to use takeover defenses as proxies for entrenchment strength, often through indices that include classified boards, staggered boards, supermajority voting requirements, limits on amending charters, golden parachutes, and poison pills [N3-F1]. Another approach is to measure entrenchment through the probability of being acquired or the likelihood of bidder behavior changing in response to defenses [N3-F1][N3-F2]. A third approach is to treat entrenchment as the ability of managers to resist replacement, which can be inferred from changes in takeover likelihood and bidder strategies [N3-F2]. The empirical evidence on costs and benefits is therefore not uniform: some studies argue that ATPs may harm firm value because they insulate managers from takeover threats, while others find that ATPs can be beneficial in contexts where internal governance is strong or where they help credibly bond firms’ commitments [N3-F1]. The same paper also notes that the effect of ATPs on firm value depends on the institutional context and that the literature is divided on whether ATPs deter takeovers and how strongly [N3-F1][N3-F2]. Overall, the evidence suggests entrenchment is best understood as a combination of board structure and takeover defense features, with empirical support for both entrenchment benefits and costs depending on governance quality and market conditions [N2-R1][N3-F1][N3-F2].

Empirical evidence on antitakeover provisions and firm value is mixed and context-dependent. The strongest evidence in the supplied material suggests that antitakeover provisions may raise firm value in some contexts, especially when internal corporate governance is sufficiently strong. In the German institutional setting, the paper finds that firms with more and stronger ATPs create value in acquisitions, with a positive valuation effect on acquirer announcement returns and a positive relationship between ATP strength and acquirer abnormal returns [N3-F1]. The paper also notes that ATPs may be especially valuable in hard-to-value industries, for firms with low bargaining power as potential takeover targets, and for firms with better management quality [N3-F1]. However, the same literature background indicates that earlier studies, including influential benchmark studies by Masulis et al. (2007) and Harford et al. (2012), argued that ATPs tend to harm firm value because they partially insulate managers from takeover threats [N3-F1]. This shows the field has been divided on whether ATPs raise or lower firm value, with the outcome depending on governance quality, market structure, and the specific provisions in place [N3-F1][N3-F2].

On takeover likelihood and bidder behavior, the evidence is similarly mixed. One study finds that voting to remove an antitakeover provision has a significant positive impact on the probability of a firm being taken over in the future, suggesting that stronger ATPs reduce takeover likelihood [N3-R4]. Another study reports that, in tests accounting for endogenous ATP use, at most 11 of 24 G-index provisions are negatively related to takeover likelihood, and only four provisions are consistently and negatively related to takeover likelihood across the 1995–2020 period [N3-F2]. Golden parachutes are positively related to takeover likelihood, indicating that not all provisions work in the same direction [N3-F2]. This implies that some provisions deter takeovers, some do not, and some may even make takeovers more likely, depending on the provision and the governance environment [N3-F2][N3-R4].

The evidence also supports a distinction between short-term and long-term market reactions. The German paper reports a positive valuation effect and higher acquirer announcement returns, which is more consistent with long-term value creation [N3-F1]. In contrast, the benchmark studies and the broader literature suggest that ATPs can create short-term discounts because they reduce the threat of replacement and may signal managerial entrenchment [N3-F1][N3-F2]. The supplied evidence therefore supports a nuanced conclusion: antitakeover provisions may raise firm value under favorable governance conditions, reduce takeover likelihood for some provisions, and have mixed short-term and long-term market implications depending on the institutional setting and the specific provisions used [N3-F1][N3-F2][N3-R4].

The strongest evidence in the supplied material is that adopting ATPs in IPO firm chapters can reduce information asymmetry by helping external investors obtain more private information, which can alleviate IPO underpricing [N4-F3]. The study also finds that the reducing effect of ATP adoption is more significant in worse information environments, suggesting that provisions can be especially valuable when market transparency is limited [N4-F3]. The evidence also indicates that IPO provisions affect investor perception and market reaction through signaling and disclosure. The study notes that ATP adoption can strengthen information disclosure and corporate transparency, which can alleviate information asymmetry between the firm and investors [N4-R1]. This implies that provisions can improve investor confidence and reduce the informational gap that often leads to underpricing [N4-R1][N4-F3]. The paper further reports that ATP adoption is associated with positive effects on IPO over-subscription, funds raised, and trading activity, while having a negative effect on listing fees [N4-F3]. Underwriter and institutional investor behavior also shape the impact of IPO provisions. The evidence also connects IPO pricing to disclosure and investor reaction, indicating that underwriters and institutional investors may respond to ATPs by adjusting pricing, demand, and market signaling [N5-R2][N5-R5]. Overall, the evidence suggests that IPO provisions can improve post-IPO shareholder returns by reducing underpricing, improving disclosure, and altering investor perception, but the effects depend on the institutional setting, the strength of the provisions, and the role of underwriters and institutional investors in shaping market reactions [N4-F3][N4-R1][N4-R2][N5-R5].

Golden parachutes also reduce takeover pressure by providing managers with generous compensation packages if they are terminated in a takeover, which can discourage bidders or make the acquisition less attractive [N1-R5]. The evidence on these provisions is not uniform, however. One study explicitly notes that classified boards do not clearly entrench managers in takeover bidding or facilitate self-dealing in that context [N2-R1], suggesting that board structure alone is not a sufficient explanation of entrenchment and that the literature remains mixed on whether these provisions truly strengthen managerial control in practice.

By reducing takeover pressure, antitakeover provisions can therefore make managers more resistant to replacement, which is a central mechanism of entrenchment [N2-R2][N2-R3]. At the same time, the evidence suggests that entrenchment is best measured as a combination of board structure and takeover defense features, rather than as a single governance variable [N3-F1]. Common measures include indices that combine classified boards, staggered boards, supermajority voting requirements, limits on amending charters, golden parachutes, and poison pills [N3-F1]. The strongest evidence in the supplied material is that adopting ATPs in IPO firm chapters can reduce information asymmetry by helping external investors obtain more private information, which can alleviate IPO underpricing [N4-F3]. This mechanism is consistent with the broader literature on information asymmetry and IPO underpricing, where information asymmetry is a key channel through which IPO firms underprice shares [N4-R2][N4-R5]. The study also finds that the reducing effect of ATP adoption is more significant in worse information environments, suggesting that provisions can be especially valuable when market transparency is limited [N4-F3]. Thus, for nonmanagerial shareholders, ATPs can indirectly improve post-IPO returns by reducing underpricing and improving pricing efficiency [N4-F3][N4-R2].

The evidence also indicates that IPO provisions affect investor perception and market reaction through signaling and disclosure. The study notes that ATP adoption can strengthen information disclosure and corporate transparency, which can alleviate information asymmetry between the firm and investors [N4-R1]. This implies that provisions can improve investor confidence and reduce the informational gap that often leads to underpricing [N4-R1][N4-F3]. The paper further reports that ATP adoption is associated with positive effects on IPO over-subscription, funds raised, and trading activity, while having a negative effect on listing fees [N4-F3]. These results suggest that nonmanagerial shareholders may benefit from better market demand and liquidity in the IPO, even as they bear some listing cost [N4-F3].

Underwriter and institutional investor behavior also shape the impact of IPO provisions. The supplied evidence shows that underwriters can affect IPO pricing considerations and that selecting underwriters with high reputations can alleviate asymmetric information and reduce IPO underpricing [N5-R5]. This implies that underwriters may help firms choose provisions that improve market signaling and investor confidence [N5-R5]. The evidence also connects IPO pricing to litigation risk and strategic disclosure, suggesting that underwriters may respond to the risk of Section 11 lawsuits by altering disclosure and pricing strategies [N5-R2]. This means underwriters may indirectly affect ATP adoption by shaping the IPO’s informational environment and the firm’s ability to attract investor demand [N5-R2].

### 4. How IPO underwriter and investor behavior shape antitakeover provision choices

IPO underwriter and investor behavior shape antitakeover provision choices primarily through reputation, pricing considerations, and information disclosure. The evidence suggests that underwriters with high reputations can alleviate asymmetric information and thus reduce IPO underpricing, implying that underwriters may help firms choose provisions that improve market signaling and investor confidence [N5-R5]. This supports the idea that underwriter reputation can influence ATP adoption because better-understood investors may be more willing to accept provisions that reduce information asymmetry [N5-R5]. The same evidence also links IPO pricing to litigation risk and strategic disclosure, suggesting that underwriters may respond to the risk of Section 11 lawsuits by altering disclosure and pricing strategies [N5-R2]. This means underwriters may indirectly affect ATP adoption by shaping the IPO’s informational environment and the firm’s ability to attract investor demand [N5-R2].

Disclosure rules and investor reaction affect signaling and information asymmetry by altering how much information investors receive about the firm. The evidence indicates that strengthening information disclosure and corporate transparency can alleviate information asymmetry between the firm and investors [N4-R1]. For IPOs, this implies that ATPs may be used not just as takeover defenses, but also as disclosure-oriented signaling mechanisms that improve market perception [N4-R1][N4-F3]. The study also finds that ATP adoption is associated with positive effects on IPO over-subscription, funds raised, and trading activity, which suggests that investor reaction can reinforce the attractiveness of provisions that improve transparency [N4-F3]. At the same time, the evidence on IPO pricing indicates that underwriters may screen IPO firms based on governance features, including ATP adoption, because better governance can lower underpricing and improve market outcomes [N5-R5]. This suggests that underwriter screening is an important channel through which investor behavior and disclosure rules shape ATP choices [N5-R5].

The evidence on post-IPO market reactions is mixed but suggestive. The IPO study finds that ATP adoption has positive effects on over-subscription, funds raised, and trading activity, which indicates strong post-IPO market reaction and demand [N4-F3]. The underwriter evidence also points to post-IPO implications through litigation risk and strategic disclosure, showing that underwriter behavior can influence both IPO pricing and long-run investor expectations [N5-R2]. Taken together, the evidence supports a picture in which underwriter reputation and IPO pricing considerations influence ATP adoption, disclosure rules and investor reaction shape signaling and information asymmetry, and underwriter screening and post-IPO market reactions provide important feedback effects on the firm’s governance choices [N5-R5][N5-R2][N4-R1][N4-F3].

### 5. Integrated conclusion

Overall, antitakeover provisions relate to managerial entrenchment by reducing takeover pressure and thereby increasing managerial control, but the evidence is mixed on whether this entrenchment is genuinely beneficial or harmful. Poison pills and golden parachutes are the most direct defenses of managerial control, while classified boards and staggered boards affect board election and strategic power more indirectly [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R4][N1-R5]. Entrenchment is measured in the literature through a combination of board structure, takeover defense features, takeover likelihood, and bidder behavior, and the empirical evidence suggests that the costs and benefits depend heavily on the institutional context and governance quality [N2-R1][N3-F1][N3-F2].

For IPO-specific effects, antitakeover provisions appear to affect nonmanagerial shareholders mainly through information asymmetry, disclosure, and investor perception. They can reduce IPO underpricing and improve pricing efficiency, especially in worse information environments, while also improving disclosure and corporate transparency [N4-F3][N4-R1][N4-R2]. Underwriters and institutional investors shape these effects through reputation, pricing considerations, and disclosure rules, which can influence both the adoption of provisions and the post-IPO market reaction [N5-R5][N5-R2]. The result is a complex relationship in which antitakeover provisions can benefit nonmanagerial shareholders by improving market transparency and demand, but they also depend on the broader governance, disclosure, and investor environment in which the IPO is placed [N4-F3][N5-R5].

In sum, the evidence supports a nuanced view: antitakeover provisions are governance tools that can reduce takeover pressure, increase managerial control, and, under favorable conditions, improve firm value and investor outcomes. But they are not universally beneficial; their effects depend on the specific provision, the governance setting, the level of information asymmetry, and the role of underwriters and institutional investors in shaping market reactions [N1-R1][N2-R2][N3-F1][N4-F3][N5-R5].
